newsitem.title: ITALY: Mafia man's "pardon" puzzles Italian investigators.
newsitem.headline: Mafia man's "pardon" puzzles Italian investigators.

text.p: Italian investigators attempted on Monday to decipher the hidden meaning of a letter written from jail by one of Sicily's most violent Mafia bosses "pardoning" his wife's killer.

The letter from Benedetto "Nitto" Santapaola, Godfather in the eastern city of Catania until his arrest in 1993, marked an unprecedented public breach of the Mafia's code of vendetta, which requires members to avenge the slaying of a relative.
It was all the more surprising for Santapaola's known devotion to his wife, Carmela Grazia, who was shot dead at her home on September 1, 1995, by two men posing as police officers.

Giuseppe Ferone, a rival Mafioso, has since confessed to the killing. His admission that he turned state's evidence and gained admission to a witness protection scheme in order to pursue a blood feud has deeply embarrassed the authorities.
"I have tried to hate Signor Ferone for the barbaric murder of my wife but I have not been able to. Nor can my sons," Santapaola wrote in a letter sent to magistrates investigating his wife's murder.
"This is not only for fear of God but also because the warm voice of my wife tells us that we should forgive," he wrote.

Anti-Mafia experts said they believed Santapaola's handwritten letter, made public as a court document in the case, might be an appeal to rival clans to halt a war for supremacy that has claimed about 70 lives in Catania this year alone.

Investigators also saw a more sinister message, with some interpreting references in the letter to days when the city was "safe" as a sign that Santapaola may be attempting to reassert his authority and undermine the state's assault on the Mob.
"Naturally, all civilised men hope that the vendettas and all other forms of violence will stop," Catania's mayor, Enzo Bianco, told reporters.
"But you cannot trust the words of a man who dominated the murky world of crime in Catania for so many years," he said.

Santapaola, nicknamed Il Cacciatore (The Hunter), bludgeoned his way to the top of the Mob, eliminating rivals as he progressed from shoe salesman to racketeer and finally a seat on the Sicilian Mafia's ruling commission.
According to turncoats, Santapaola crossed swords with "boss of bosses" Salvatore Riina, also arrested in 1993, by opposing Riina's strategy of all-out war on the state.
Riina appeared in court in Caltanissetta, central Sicily, on Monday for the start of his trial with 17 other alleged Mafiosi for the murder in 1992 of star magistrate Paolo Borsellino.
Borsellino and five policemen were blown up by a car bomb in the Sicilian capital Palermo in July 1992 two months after the killing of Borsellino's close colleague Giovanni Falcone.
The two killings galvanised the state into a serious crackdown on organised crime, with Riina, Santapaola and a host of other top mobsters netted in the assault.
Santapaola is a co-defendant with Riina at the trial over Falcone's murder but is not accused in the Borsellino affair.
Tales from his bloodthirsty past have added to the scepticism felt by investigators about his letter from jail.
According to a leading turncoat, Antonio Calderone, he had four boys, one only 12 years old, strangled and thrown down a well in the mid-1970s for snatching his mother's handbag.
Calderone also alleges that Santapaola once sent two mobsters to kneecap a driving instructor who had flirted with his wife. They got the wrong man and wounded his brother.
